positions.claim: Cheaper code generation does not automatically make code review cheaper, so verification is now the bottleneck rather than production.
Clean, maintainable repos do not improve agent pass rates but do reduce token usage and revisits, so maintainability pays off as efficiency.
Roughly 96% of engineers do not fully trust AI-generated code, but only about half always verify it before committing.
Taste is not a durable moat — it is alpha that decays as models learn from examples and preferences, just more slowly than speed or recall.
'What can the agent do?' is no longer a useful strategic question because the list of things agents can't do keeps shrinking; the better question is what only a human can be answerable for.
Running more agents in parallel does not increase your effective capacity, because human cognitive bandwidth does not parallelize and each loop adds routing, merging, and verification decisions.
The half-life of any individual capability edge is about one model release, while the half-life of credibility and accountability is much longer.
Agents can legitimately choose, route, merge, and escalate inside policy, but execution and responsibility are categorically different and responsibility cannot be delegated to an agent.
Code should not ship unless some human can explain it well enough to defend it, even if no human typed or read every line.
Lowering the cost of building software has historically increased rather than decreased demand for it, and agents will follow the same pattern.
Organizational governance of AI-assisted code is lagging behind adoption, making review and validation an institutional bottleneck rather than just an individual one.
High agency in an agent-heavy world means deciding which problems deserve your ownership, not personally executing everything.
The distinction between an agent and a harness is pedantic and the two can be conflated in practice.
The reason organizations build custom agents is data integration, not dissatisfaction with existing general-purpose AI products.
There is currently no defined, standard way to build an agent; Vercel's Eve is the closest thing.
MCP has succeeded only as a tool distribution mechanism and has not delivered value beyond tools, as shown by tools being the only fully supported column on MCP's own client support matrix.
Installing many skills into one agent measurably degrades its performance.
Loading skills, MCP servers, and tools into a single agent's context is functionally inheritance, and like inheritance it hits diminishing returns and eventually breaks down.
Sub-agents should communicate with their coordinator in natural English rather than a structured protocol.
Domain-specific agents deliver over 80% token efficiency for a given task compared to the general-purpose alternative.
DeepSeek V4 Flash is 137 times cheaper per task than Fable 5, and narrow task scoping makes the cheaper model reliable enough to use.
Narrow, capability-limited agents are a better answer to the permission-bypass problem than permission dialogs on a maximally capable coding agent.
Domain-specific agents do not meaningfully exist in public today.
Adoption of domain-specific agents will accelerate rapidly through the second half of 2026, and 2027 will be the year of multi-agent orchestration.
The cost of intelligence stopped falling and reversed in 2026: tokens are up 76% raw and 29% IQ-adjusted at the halfway point of the year.
Frontier models like Fable are too expensive to place in front of customers unless those customers have very high lifetime value.
A sandboxed filesystem and sandboxed code execution should be built-in primitives of every domain-specific agent, not optional add-ons.
Full agents, not just functions, should be usable as tools within another agent, allowing recursive sub-agent hierarchies.
Because each domain-specific agent is a small isolated execution environment, thousands can be run in parallel across regions without heavy shared infrastructure.
